planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil; this old, widely grown selection roots readily from stem cuttings and will climb by clinging rootlets if given a wall or trunk, or stay low and trailing if left unsupported.

directions: One of the oldest and most widely planted wintercreeper selections, this cultivar bears small oval leaves edged in creamy white with an occasional pink flush in cold weather, giving a lighter, airier look than solid-green wintercreeper. It tolerates deep shade better than most variegated groundcovers, though the white margins are crisper with a few hours of filtered sun. Left untrained it forms a dense trailing mat useful for covering slopes and difficult shaded banks; given a wall, fence, or tree trunk it climbs by clinging aerial roots like ivy. Established plantings need only an occasional shearing to control spread and remove any plain-green reverted shoots.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in average, well-drained soil; Harlequin is markedly slower and more compact than most wintercreeper cultivars, so set plants closer together than usual if a filled-in look is wanted within a few seasons.

directions: Harlequin carries the heaviest white speckling of any common wintercreeper, with scalloped leaves so densely mottled in white and patched in yellow-green that whole stem tips can appear almost pure white, especially on new growth. This intense variegation comes at the cost of vigor — it is a slow, dwarf, mounding grower well suited to rock gardens, edging, and small-space accents rather than fast groundcover coverage. Leaves take on a rosy blush in cold weather, adding winter interest to its pale coloring. Because so little chlorophyll is present in the whitest shoots, any branches that revert to solid green should be pruned out to keep the plant from being overtaken by its more vigorous all-green growth.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Ivory Jade spreads as a dense, ground-hugging mound and benefits from an early spring shearing to keep margins tidy and encourage fresh new-growth color.

directions: Ivory Jade was selected for improved cold hardiness over similar white-margined wintercreepers, holding its rich green-and-ivory leaf coloring through winters where comparable selections can suffer dieback. The ivory margins often take on a soft pink tinge once temperatures drop, adding seasonal color to what is otherwise a steady, low, ground-hugging mound of foliage. It brightens shaded corners and foundation plantings that would otherwise read as a dark wall of green, and its dense habit suppresses weeds effectively once established. Light shearing in late winter keeps the mound compact and removes any winter-damaged tips before new growth begins.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Sparkle 'n Gold forms a broader mound than Emerald 'n Gold and holds its gold margins well even where afternoon shade limits direct sun.

directions: Sparkle 'n Gold bears noticeably larger leaves than Emerald 'n Gold, each with a deep green center broadly edged in bright yellow that shifts toward pink and bronze tones as temperatures drop in fall and winter. The larger leaf size gives plantings a bolder, coarser texture than finer-leaved wintercreeper cultivars, making it useful as a accent mound or low hedge rather than a tight weed-suppressing mat. It tolerates shearing well if a more formal, rounded shape is desired, and its orange fall capsules add a secondary season of interest. Established plants are tough and adaptable, shrugging off heat, drought, and poor soil once rooted in.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Minimus stays low and ground-hugging unless given something to climb, making it a reliable filler between stepping stones or over rock garden edges.

directions: Baby wintercreeper carries the smallest leaves of any common fortunei selection, forming a tight, fine-textured mat only a few inches tall that can spread considerably wider over time. Its diminutive scale makes it a good choice for rock gardens, trough plantings, and small spaces where larger wintercreeper cultivars would overwhelm the setting. It tolerates everything from full sun to deep shade and adapts to most soils once established, though it spreads vigorously enough that gardeners in mild, humid regions should edge or contain plantings to keep it from wandering into adjoining beds or lawn. Occasional shearing keeps the mat dense and prevents it from mounding up where it is not wanted.
sources: Morton Arboretum Plant and Protect Guide
North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Wolong Ghost Wintercreeper (Silver-Veined Dan Hinkley Introduction)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this selection stays low and spreading unless given a wall or trunk to climb, and performs well cascading over the edge of a raised bed or container.

directions: Wolong Ghost was collected by plantsman Dan Hinkley on an expedition to the Wolong Nature Reserve in Sichuan, China, and brought into the North American nursery trade as a distinctive shade groundcover. Its dark evergreen leaves are overlaid with a silvery, almost ghostly network of veining that reads as a soft gray-green haze from a distance rather than the bold white edging typical of most variegated wintercreepers. It thrives in deep shade where few broadleaf evergreen groundcovers hold good color, forming a dense, weed-suppressing mat over time. Left unpruned it will also climb a nearby trunk or wall by clinging rootlets, giving gardeners a choice between a flat groundcover and a textured vertical accent.

common_name: Green Carpet Periwinkle (Dense Compact Vinca Minor)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Green Carpet's tighter habit and smaller leaves mean it takes slightly longer to knit into a solid mat than larger-leaved vinca minor selections, so plant it a little closer than usual for faster coverage.

directions: Green Carpet is a fine-textured, low-growing selection of common periwinkle, with smaller leaves and a denser, flatter habit than the species, forming an unusually tight evergreen mat under trees and shrubs. Pale lavender-blue flowers appear in modest numbers in spring, but this selection is grown primarily for its foliage density and uniform low profile rather than for bloom display. Its compact scale makes it a good choice for small shaded beds, foundation plantings, and areas where a tidier, less rambunctious groundcover than standard vinca minor is wanted. Once established it tolerates a wide range of soils and needs little more than an annual trim to keep edges in bounds.
